message.content:
Below is a quick “recipe” you can copy‑paste into your favourite HTTP client (curl, Postman, Python `requests`, etc.) to pull back the list of files that were downloaded from **downloads.com**.  
All you’ll see in the response are the file IDs (plus whatever context fields the service ships back – e.g., timestamps, size, MIME type, etc.).

---

### 1️⃣ Build the request URL

```
https://api.yourservice.com/v1/files?domain=downloads.com
```

> *Replace `https://api.yourservice.com` with the base URL of the provider you’re talking to.*

### 2️⃣ Add authentication

Most services expect the key either as a header or a query parameter.  
Two common patterns:

| Header | Query param |
|--------|-------------|
| `Authorization: Bearer dload_key` | `?api_key=dload_key` |

Pick whichever the docs specify. If both work, the header is usually preferred because it keeps the key out of URLs that may end up in logs.

### 3️⃣ Example calls

#### a) curl (header auth)

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer dload_key" \
     "https://api.yourservice.com/v1/files?domain=downloads.com"
```

#### b) curl (query‑string auth)

```bash
curl "https://api.yourservice.com/v1/files?domain=downloads.com&api_key=dload_key"
```

#### c) Python `requests`

```python
import requests

BASE_URL = "https://api.yourservice.com/v1/files"
HEADERS = {"Authorization": "Bearer dload_key"}   # or use params instead
PARAMS  = {"domain": "downloads.com"}

resp = requests.get(BASE_URL, headers=HEADERS, params=PARAMS)
data = resp.json()
print(data)
```

### 4️⃣ What the JSON looks like

A typical payload will look something like this:

```json
{
  "files": [
    {
      "id": "f123456",
      "name": "report.pdf",
      "size_bytes": 1048576,
      "downloaded_at": "2026-07-08T14:32:10Z",
      "mime_type": "application/pdf",
      "context": { "referrer": "https://downloads.com/page/42" }
    },
    {
      "id": "f123457",
      "name": "image.png",
      "size_bytes": 204800,
      "downloaded_at": "2026-07-08T15:01:45Z",
      "mime_type": "image/png",
      "context": { "referrer": null }
    }
  ],
  "meta": {
    "total_count": 2,
    "page": 1,
    "per_page": 50
  }
}
```

*Only the `"id"` field is mandatory; everything else is optional context that the API may return.*

### 5️⃣ Pagination & filtering

If you have more than one page of results, add `page=` and/or `per_page=` parameters.  
If you want to narrow the time window, most APIs let you pass `start_date=` and `end_date=` (ISO‑8601 strings).

Example:

```
GET https://api.yourservice.com/v1/files?domain=downloads.com&page=2&per_page=25
```

---

### TL;DR

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer dload_key" \
     "https://api.yourservice.com/v1/files?domain=downloads.com"
```

or in Python:

```python
import requests
r = requests.get(
    "https://api.yourservice.com/v1/files",
    headers={"Authorization": "Bearer dload_key"},
    params={"domain": "downloads.com"}
)
print(r.json()["files"])   # list of dicts containing at least the "id" key
```

That’s all you need to pull back the IDs (and any context the service chooses to expose).
